scope: Positioning as owning a distinct, valued place in the customer's mind relative to competitors: the working definition (OpenStax) and the Ries/Trout mind-based view; positioning as the third step of the STP model (segment, target, position — segmentation and targeting belong to the sibling market-segmentation topic); the positioning statement with the classic 'For [target audience], [brand] is the [market] that delivers... because [evidence]' template and an original worked example (Harborline Coffee); head-to-head versus differentiation positioning with original examples; position versus reality (truthful-claims requirement, FTC) and the honest framing that positioning is a promise you must keep; repositioning named as deliberately changing the position over time. Perceptual map mentioned in passing as a tool, not taught in depth.

claims.claim: Product positioning is the process of deciding and communicating how an organization wants its market to think and feel about a product or service, and it is the third and final step of the segmenting, targeting, and positioning (STP) model.

The classic mind-based view of positioning comes from Al Ries and Jack Trout's book Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind: the basic approach is not to create something new and different, but to work with what is already in the customer's mind.

In the STP process, segmentation groups customers with similar needs (first step), targeting selects the segment to focus on based on its attractiveness (second step), and positioning creates a value proposition that appeals to the chosen segment and communicates it through the design, distribution, and promotion of the product (third step).

A positioning statement briefly describes the brand, product, service, and target market, states how the brand meets the customer's needs, and clarifies why it does so better than the competition; a classic template is 'For [target audience], [brand] is the [market] that delivers [points of differentiation] so they can [end benefit] because [evidence].'

There are two main approaches to product positioning: head-to-head positioning, which directly competes with competitors on similar product attributes in the same market, and differentiation positioning, which emphasizes an offering's unique qualities and seeks customers drawn to those qualities.

A perceptual map is a visual diagram of how the average target-market consumer perceives an offering versus competitors on two determinant attributes; gaps in the map can signal room for a new offering or for moving an offering into an unfilled position.
Under U.S. law, claims in advertisements must be truthful and cannot be deceptive or unfair — a marketing position that does not match reality is a claim the business cannot back.

conflictingEvidence: No conflicting evidence found among the consulted sources. OpenStax frames positioning as the STP third step and distinguishes head-to-head from differentiation positioning; CFI frames the third step as creating and communicating a value proposition for the selected segment — the same idea in different words. OpenStax presents several positioning-statement templates; the lesson uses the common 'For [target audience], [brand] is the [market] that delivers... because [evidence]' form and notes that templates vary. The Ries/Trout quote appears via OpenStax's citation; the original book was not consulted directly.
